Subject: Change to your flight BF 482

Dear Ms. Kobayashi,

The departure time of your flight from Denver to Seattle on June 14 has changed. Flight BF 482 will now leave at 4:55 p.m. instead of 2:10 p.m. because of a change to our summer schedule. Your seat, 17C, and your checked bag allowance remain the same.

router.subject: Psychology
router.title: How Habits Take Hold
paragraphs: A habit is a behavior that a person performs almost automatically, with little conscious thought. Brushing one's teeth, locking the door, and checking a phone on waking are familiar examples. Psychologists describe a habit as a loop with three parts: a cue that triggers the behavior, the routine itself, and a reward that makes the brain want to repeat it.

Habits form through repetition in a stable setting. Each time a routine follows the same cue and brings a reward, the link between them grows stronger, until the cue alone is enough to start the action. This takes longer than many people assume. In one well-known study at a London university, volunteers needed about two months, on average, before a new daily behavior felt automatic, and some needed far longer. Missing a single day, however, did not noticeably slow their progress.

Because habits are tied to cues, they are hard to break by willpower alone. An old routine tends to return whenever the familiar cue appears, especially when a person is tired or under stress. For this reason, psychologists often advise changing the surroundings instead: keeping snacks out of sight, for instance, or taking a different route home. Research on people who have just moved suggests the same thing. In a new place, the old cues are missing, so old routines are easier to replace.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why some people are born with more willpower than others
How scientists measure behavior that is automatic
How habits are built and why they are hard to change
Why bad habits are more common than good ones
questions.why: Paragraphs 1 and 2 explain what a habit is and how repetition builds it; paragraph 3 explains why habits 'are hard to break by willpower alone'.

questions.q: According to the passage, what did the study of volunteers show?
options: Forming a habit took about two months on average.
Most volunteers gave up before the study had ended.
Missing a single day forced volunteers to start again.
Rewards had little effect on how quickly habits formed.
questions.why: 'Volunteers needed about two months, on average, before a new daily behavior felt automatic.' Missing one day 'did not noticeably slow their progress'.

questions.q: The word "triggers" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: follows
prevents
rewards
sets off
questions.why: A cue that triggers a behavior starts it, or sets it off.

questions.q: Why does the author mention people who have just moved?
options: To show that moving to a new home is a stressful experience
To support the idea that habits weaken when their cues are absent
To argue that willpower is stronger in unfamiliar places
To give an example of a habit that takes months to form
questions.why: 'In a new place, the old cues are missing, so old routines are easier to replace.' The example backs up the advice to change the surroundings.

questions.q: According to the passage, all of the following are true of habits EXCEPT:
options: They are carried out with little thought.
They grow stronger through repetition.
They fade when a person is tired.
They are linked to particular cues.
questions.why: The passage says the opposite of C: an old routine tends to return 'especially when a person is tired or under stress'. A, B and D are stated in paragraphs 1, 2 and 3.

upper.subject: History of science
upper.title: Penicillin and the Rise of Resistance
paragraphs: In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned from a holiday to find that mold had grown on one of the dishes in which he was raising bacteria. Around the mold, the bacteria had died. Fleming named the substance responsible penicillin, but he could not produce enough of it to treat patients. That step was taken more than a decade later by a team at Oxford that included Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, and by the mid-1940s factories were turning out the drug in enormous quantities.

Penicillin transformed medicine. Infections that had often been fatal could now be cured within days. Yet Fleming himself sounded a warning. Accepting the Nobel Prize in 1945, he pointed out that careless use of the drug might allow bacteria to become resistant to it.

His fear proved justified. In any large population of bacteria, a few may happen to carry a trait that lets them survive a drug. When an antibiotic kills their competitors, these survivors multiply and pass the trait on. The more widely antibiotics are used, therefore, the more chances resistant strains have to spread. Today some infections no longer respond to drugs that once cured them easily, and few new antibiotics have reached the market in recent decades. The discovery that seemed to defeat bacterial disease turned out to be only the opening move in a much longer contest.

questions.q: According to the passage, why was penicillin not used to treat patients soon after its discovery?
options: Doctors doubted that a mold could cure infections.
Fleming was unable to make it in sufficient amounts.
The first tests on bacteria gave disappointing results.
Factories were busy producing other medicines.
questions.why: Paragraph 1: Fleming 'could not produce enough of it to treat patients'; the Oxford team solved that more than a decade later.

questions.q: The word "fatal" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: painful
common
lasting
deadly
questions.why: A fatal infection is one that kills; the sentence contrasts such infections with ones that can 'be cured within days'.

questions.q: Why does the author mention what Fleming said when he accepted the Nobel Prize?
options: To show that the risk of resistance was recognized very early
To prove that Fleming deserved more credit than the Oxford team
To explain how penicillin came to be produced in factories
To suggest that the prize was awarded too soon
questions.why: Already in 1945 Fleming 'pointed out that careless use of the drug might allow bacteria to become resistant'; paragraph 3 begins 'His fear proved justified.'

questions.q: According to the passage, how does resistance spread among bacteria?
options: Bacteria learn to avoid the places where drugs are used.
Antibiotics lose their strength when stored for too long.
Surviving bacteria reproduce and hand down their advantage.
Mold gradually stops making the substance that kills bacteria.
questions.why: Paragraph 3: a few bacteria carry a trait that lets them survive, and 'these survivors multiply and pass the trait on'.

questions.q: What does the author imply by describing penicillin as "the opening move in a much longer contest"?
options: Scientists competed fiercely to be the first to discover it.
The struggle between medicine and bacteria is still going on.
Other antibiotics had been discovered before penicillin.
Bacterial disease will soon be defeated completely.
questions.why: An opening move is only the start of a game. Bacteria keep adapting and few new drugs are appearing, so the contest has not ended.

router.subject: Architecture
router.script: Here's something that might surprise you. If you stand at the top of a very tall building on a windy day, the floor under your feet is moving. Skyscrapers sway. The very tallest can move a meter or more in a storm, and they're designed to. A tower that can bend a little is actually safer than one that can't. So the real problem for engineers isn't keeping the building up. It's keeping the people inside comfortable, because nobody wants to feel seasick at their desk. So, how do they do it? One answer is shape. When wind flows around a square tower, it breaks into swirls of air that push the building from side to side. Rounded corners, or an outline that changes as the tower rises, break up those swirls before they get strong. The Burj Khalifa in Dubai does exactly that. Its outline keeps changing on the way up, so the wind never gets organized. A second answer is weight. Near the top of Taipei 101, in Taiwan, there's an enormous steel ball, more than six hundred tons of it, hanging from cables. When the wind pushes the tower one way, the ball swings the other way and absorbs much of the movement. And it isn't hidden. Visitors can go and look at it. For next time, I'd like each of you to find one more building that uses a trick like this.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Ways of reducing the movement of tall buildings in wind
Reasons why modern towers are taller than older ones
The history of the world's most famous skyscrapers
How engineers measure the speed of the wind
questions.why: After explaining that towers sway, the professor asks 'how do they do it?' and gives two answers: shape and weight.

Keeping the windows from breaking
Making sure people inside do not feel sick

questions.why: 'The real problem for engineers isn't keeping the building up. It's keeping the people inside comfortable, because nobody wants to feel seasick.'

router.subject: Agriculture
router.script: Today's topic is a farming idea that's thousands of years old and still in use: crop rotation. The idea is simple. You don't grow the same crop in the same field year after year. Why not? Well, think about what happens if you plant wheat again and again. Wheat takes a lot of nitrogen out of the soil, so each harvest gets a little smaller. And the insects and diseases that like wheat stay right there in the field, waiting for next year's meal. Now, farmers long ago knew nothing about nitrogen, but they could see the results. In medieval Europe, many villages divided their land into three big fields, and each year one of the three was left empty to rest. It worked. But notice the cost. A third of the land grew nothing. The real breakthrough, which spread across England in the seventeen hundreds, was a four-year rotation. Two of the years were for grain. In the other two, farmers grew turnips and clover. No resting year at all. How was that possible? Clover belongs to the same family as peas and beans, and bacteria living on the roots of these plants take nitrogen from the air and put it back into the soil. So the clover was feeding the field. And the turnips and clover also fed the farm animals through the winter, which meant more animals and more manure for the soil. More food from the same land. Not bad for a simple change of plan.

options: Why wheat became the most important crop in Europe
How medieval villages shared their farmland
How farm animals were kept alive through the winter

questions.why: The topic is named at the start, 'crop rotation', and the talk explains why it works and how it improved.

options: It required too many farm animals.
Part of the land produced no food each year.

questions.why: 'It worked, but notice the cost. A third of the land grew nothing.'

questions.q: What does the professor say about clover?
options: It helps return nitrogen to the soil.

questions.why: Bacteria on the roots of clover 'take nitrogen from the air and put it back into the soil. So the clover was feeding the field.'

questions.q: Why does the professor say this: "Not bad for a simple change of plan"?
options: To admit that the four-year rotation had some weaknesses
To suggest that farmers disliked changing their methods
To stress how much was gained from a small idea
To remind students that the plan is no longer used
questions.why: 'Not bad' is understatement: he has just listed the gains ('more food from the same land') that came from merely changing the order of crops.

upper.subject: Physics
upper.script: Why is the sky blue? It sounds like a child's question, and that's exactly why I like it, because most adults can't answer it. A surprising number will tell you, quite confidently, that the sky reflects the ocean. It doesn't. So let's do this properly. Sunlight looks white, but it's really a mixture of every color, and each color travels as a wave of a different length. Red waves are long. Blue and violet waves are short. Now, the air is full of gas molecules, far smaller than any of those waves, and when sunlight hits them, it gets scattered, sent off in all directions. But not equally. Short waves are scattered far more strongly than long ones. So blue light ends up bouncing around the whole sky and reaching your eyes from every direction, while most of the red passes straight through. We call this Rayleigh scattering, after the British physicist who worked out the mathematics in the nineteenth century. Now, some of you are already thinking, hang on, violet is even shorter than blue, so why isn't the sky violet? Good. Partly, the sun gives off less violet to begin with, and partly, our eyes just aren't very sensitive to it. And sunsets? At the end of the day, sunlight has to cross far more air to reach you. By then, most of the blue has been scattered out of the beam, and what's left is orange and red.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How the human eye tells colors apart
How scattered sunlight gives the sky its color
Why the ocean and the sky are the same color
How a physicist measured the length of light waves
questions.why: The professor answers her opening question, 'Why is the sky blue?', with the scattering of sunlight by air molecules.

questions.q: What is the professor's attitude toward the idea that the sky reflects the ocean?
options: She thinks it is partly correct.
She is unsure whether it has been tested.
She finds it a useful way to teach children.
She considers it a widespread mistake.
questions.why: 'A surprising number will tell you, quite confidently, that the sky reflects the ocean. It doesn't.'

questions.q: According to the professor, why does blue light reach our eyes from every part of the sky?
options: Air molecules scatter short waves more than long ones.
Blue light travels faster than red light.
The sun produces more blue light than any other color.
Blue waves are too long to pass through the air.
questions.why: 'Short waves are scattered far more strongly than long ones. So blue light ends up bouncing around the whole sky.'

questions.q: Why does the professor bring up violet light?
options: To correct a mistake in Rayleigh's mathematics
To show that sunsets contain every color
To answer a question students are likely to ask
To prove that human eyes cannot see short waves
questions.why: 'Some of you are already thinking, hang on, violet is even shorter than blue, so why isn't the sky violet?' She raises the objection herself and answers it.

upper.subject: Linguistics
upper.script: There are roughly seven thousand languages spoken in the world today. By the end of this century, by many estimates, around half of them will have fallen silent. Now, I want to be careful here, because people tend to picture this the wrong way. Languages rarely die because their speakers die. They die because parents, usually for perfectly sensible reasons, stop passing them on. If the language of school, of work, of the city is something else, then speaking that other language to your children looks like giving them a head start. Nobody decides to kill a language. It just isn't handed down. And one generation is all it takes. So what, you might say. Wouldn't life be simpler with fewer languages? Well, consider what goes with them. A community that has lived in one place for centuries has names for plants, for animals, for kinds of weather, that often exist nowhere else and were never written down. And for us linguists, every language is a piece of evidence about what the human mind can do. Lose it, and that evidence is gone for good. It isn't hopeless, though. In New Zealand in the nineteen eighties, Māori communities began running preschools, called language nests, where small children heard nothing but Māori all day. The idea has since been copied elsewhere, including Hawaii. It doesn't guarantee survival. But it does show that the decline is not a law of nature.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How linguists count the world's languages
Why children learn languages faster than adults
How the Māori language spread to Hawaii
Why languages disappear and why it matters
questions.why: The professor explains how languages are lost (they are not passed on), what is lost with them, and one attempt to stop the decline.

questions.q: According to the professor, what usually causes a language to disappear?
options: Its speakers are forbidden to use it.
It is no longer taught to the next generation.
Its vocabulary becomes too old-fashioned.
Its last speakers move to other countries.
questions.why: 'They die because parents, usually for perfectly sensible reasons, stop passing them on.'

questions.q: Why does the professor say this: "So what, you might say. Wouldn't life be simpler with fewer languages?"
options: To raise an objection that he then answers
To show that he agrees with this view
To ask the students to vote on the question
To suggest that the estimates are exaggerated
questions.why: He voices a doubt a listener might have and at once replies, 'Well, consider what goes with them.'

questions.q: What is the professor's view of the language nests?
options: They have solved the problem in New Zealand.
They are encouraging, though not a certain solution.
They work only for languages with written records.
They are too expensive to copy in other places.
questions.why: 'It doesn't guarantee survival. But it does show that the decline is not a law of nature.'

professor.name: Dr. Halvorsen
professor.post: This week we are studying how governments try to influence what people eat and drink. Dozens of countries, including Mexico and the United Kingdom, now place a special tax on sugary drinks. Supporters argue that higher prices lead people to consume less sugar and that the money can pay for health programs. Critics reply that such taxes fall hardest on families with low incomes and that people should be free to choose. What is your view? Should governments tax sugary drinks? Why or why not?

students.name: Renata
students.post: I support the tax. When something costs more, people buy less of it, and that is especially true of teenagers, who have little money of their own. A tax also pushes companies to put less sugar in their products so that they pay less. A small change in price seems to me an easy way to protect children.

students.name: Callum
students.post: I don't think a tax is the right tool. Rich people will hardly notice a few extra cents, so the cost falls mostly on poorer families. Besides, people can simply switch to other sweet foods. I would rather see governments spend money on education and on free drinking water in every school.

discussion.model: I believe governments should tax sugary drinks, but only if the tax is designed carefully. Callum is right that a higher price is harder on families with little money. However, those same families often suffer most from the health problems connected with too much sugar, so they also have the most to gain. To make the policy fair, the money collected should go back to the communities that pay it, for example by lowering the price of fruit and vegetables or by putting free water fountains in public places. I would also add an idea that has not been mentioned: the tax could depend on the amount of sugar in each drink rather than on the size of the bottle. Then companies would have a strong reason to change their recipes, and people could keep buying their favorite brands in a healthier form.

interview.scenario: You have agreed to take part in a research study about friendship and keeping in touch. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

questions.q: Thank you for joining me today. I'd like to start with your own experience. Think of a friend you don't see very often. How did the two of you meet, and how do you stay in contact now?
questions.model: One friend I don't see very often is Mateo. We met on the first day of high school, because the teacher gave us seats next to each other. We soon discovered that we supported the same football team, and after that we spent almost every weekend together. Two years ago, he moved to another city to study engineering, so now we mostly keep in touch online. We send each other short voice messages a few times a week, usually about football or something funny that happened. About once a month we have a long video call, and during the holidays we always try to meet in person.

questions.q: Some people like to have a large circle of friends, while others prefer just a few close ones. Which is closer to your own preference, and why?
questions.model: I definitely prefer having a few close friends. For me, friendship takes time, and I only have a limited amount of it because of my studies and my part-time job. If I tried to stay close to twenty people, I would not be able to give any of them real attention. With my three best friends, I can talk about serious things, such as family problems or worries about the future, and I know they will listen. Of course, I enjoy meeting new people in class, and I am friendly with many of them. But I would call them acquaintances rather than true friends.

questions.q: Now I'd like to hear your opinion. Some people believe that a friendship cannot really stay strong when two friends live far away from each other. Do you agree or disagree? Why?
questions.model: I disagree with that view. Distance certainly makes a friendship harder, because you cannot share everyday moments, like eating lunch together. However, I think the strength of a friendship depends on effort, not on location. My cousin and her best friend have lived in different countries for ten years, and they are still very close because they call each other every Sunday. In some ways, distance can even improve a friendship, since people stop taking each other for granted. On the other hand, if neither person makes time for the other, the friendship will fade, even if they live on the same street.

questions.q: Here is my last question. Many students move to a new city for university and find it hard to make friends there. Do you think universities should do more to help new students build friendships, or is that the students' own responsibility? Please explain.
questions.model: I think universities should do more, although students also have to make an effort. Starting university can be very lonely, especially for students who come from another city or country and know nobody. Loneliness affects their health and their grades, so it is in the university's interest to help. For example, universities could organize small group activities in the first weeks, such as hiking trips or cooking evenings, instead of only big welcome parties where shy people feel lost. They could also match each new student with an older student from the same department. After that first step, it is up to the students to keep the friendships going.
